## Simple explanation

Neural architecture search (NAS) uses an algorithm to explore possible
neural network designs instead of relying entirely on a person to choose
each layer and connection.

## Technical explanation

NAS defines a search space of candidate architectures, a strategy for
selecting candidates, and an evaluation procedure. Search strategies include
random search, evolutionary methods, reinforcement learning, and
differentiable relaxations. The objective may combine validation quality
with latency, memory, or energy constraints.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

NAS can help tailor models to a task or deployment target, including
resource-limited devices. It can also be extremely costly and its result is
only as useful as the search space, data, and evaluation protocol.

## How it works

The search process proposes an architecture, trains or estimates its
performance, and uses that result to guide later candidates. Some methods
train candidates independently; weight-sharing approaches reuse parameters
to reduce cost but can make candidate rankings less reliable. The final
architecture should be retrained and evaluated independently.

## Practical example

A team deploying image classification on a mobile device could search
within a constrained set of convolutional and attention blocks, optimizing
for validation accuracy while requiring inference latency below a target
on the actual device.

## Common misconceptions

- NAS does not guarantee a better design than careful manual engineering.
- Search results depend on the search space and evaluation setup.
- A proxy metric or hardware simulator may not predict real deployment cost accurately.
